title="Chapter overview"} Chapters 7 and 8 fitted lines and additive models and read them as conditional comparisons. Along the way they used tools they could only name: a factor coded as 0/1 columns, a contrast between two categories, a joint test of several added coefficients, an information criterion, a squared predictor, a logged outcome, a covariance estimate that allows unequal spread, and a covariance that respects pupils sitting in schools. This chapter develops each of them once, on the same 98 occupation records, on a small randomized reading study with a pretest, and on Project STAR, a randomized class-size study in which pupils sit in schools. By the end of the chapter you will be able to code and read a factor with several levels, estimate a contrast with the right uncertainty, read an analysis of covariance as a regression on a randomized pretest--posttest study, compare nested models and read AIC and BIC, change a predictor's form or an outcome's scale and say what question changed, choose between classical, HC3, cluster-robust, and bootstrap uncertainty for a stated reason, and say what none of these calculations repairs. ::: A regression report rarely stops at one additive equation, and this chapter takes the usual further steps in order. Section 1 enters a factor as indicator columns and shows that the one-way analysis of variance is that regression. Section 2 compares groups through contrasts and then adjusts a randomized comparison for a pretest, the analysis of covariance. Section 3 compares nested models, and Section 4 changes a predictor's form or the outcome's scale. Sections 5 and 6 recalculate the uncertainty when the spread is unequal, by a robust covariance and by resampling, and Section 7 meets a design in which pupils sit in schools, so that the uncertainty has to follow the schools. Each step has a common misreading: taking a coefficient as "the effect of type", adding two standard errors, comparing criteria across different outcomes, or treating a robust standard error as a repair for a design problem. The occupation records of Chapter 8 carry most of the work: 98 complete rows, income in thousand 1971 Canadian dollars, and the additive model of education, prestige, percentage of women, and type, with the type levels *bc*, *prof*, and *wc*. Every tool is therefore seen on numbers already read, and every adjusted type comparison holds education, prestige, and the percentage of women fixed. The R code shown is the one call that produces each new quantity; the Computer Lab carries the preparation, the checks, and the variations. Where Chapter 8's appendices already worked a tool through on these records (the group means recovered by indicators, the overall $F$, the HC3 covariance, and the Normal likelihood behind AIC and BIC), this chapter points back and adds the new use. \clearpage ## Predictors That Are Categories {#sec-ch9-factors} ### One indicator, then several Chapter 7, Section 3.3, fitted a single 0/1 predictor to 24 invented feedback-by-practice scores. The fitted line passed through the two group means, its slope was their difference, 4 with SE 1.6967 and $t=2.3575$ on 22 df, and that test was the equal-variance two-sample test written as a regression. The same idea extends to more than two groups. A factor with $J$ levels enters a regression as $J-1$ indicator columns. One level is omitted and becomes the **reference**: the intercept is its fitted mean, and each indicator coefficient is a difference from it. With three occupation types and blue-collar as the reference, $$ \widehat y_g=\widehat\alpha+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}} +\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}},\qquad \widehat\mu_{\mathrm{bc}}=\widehat\alpha,\quad \widehat\mu_{\mathrm{prof}}=\widehat\alpha+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}},\quad \widehat\mu_{\mathrm{wc}}=\widehat\alpha+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}. $$ Two indicators, not three, carry three means. A third column would equal the intercept column minus the other two, so the design matrix would lose full rank and no coefficient would be separately estimable. Which level is omitted is a choice of coordinates, not a choice of model. The Chapter 8 records and models are re-created here so that every later calculation has a stated origin: `m0`, `m1`, and `m2` are the education-only, the education-and-prestige, and the full additive models. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prestige <- carData::Prestige prestige$income_k <- prestige$income / 1000 d <- prestige[!is.na(prestige$type), ] d$type <- factor(d$type, levels = c("bc", "prof", "wc")) m0 <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = d) m1 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige, data = d) m2 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type, data = d) ``` ::: The 98 records hold 44 blue-collar, 31 professional, and 23 white-collar occupations, and the full model fits six coefficients, leaving 92 residual degrees of freedom. The rows were chosen because their records are complete, not sampled at random from a labour market [@carData2022; @fox2019]. ### What the indicator coefficients mean Fit income on type alone and read the coefficients against @fig-ch9-indicators. A blue-collar occupation carries 0 in both indicator columns, a professional one a 1 in the first, and a white-collar one a 1 in the second, so each type's fitted value is the intercept plus that type's coefficient. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} group_fit <- lm(income_k ~ type, data = d) coef(group_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) typeprof typewc 5.374136 5.185315 -0.321832 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Income of the 98 occupations by type. Bars mark the group means; the dashed line is the blue-collar mean, the intercept, and the arrows are the two indicator coefficients, 5.1853 and −0.3218.](chapter_09_files/figure-html/fig-ch9-indicators-1.png){#fig-ch9-indicators fig-pos='!ht' fig-alt='Jittered open circles of income in thousand dollars for 44 blue-collar, 31 professional and 23 white-collar occupations, with a thick bar at each group mean, about 5.37, 10.56 and 5.05. A dashed horizontal line at the blue-collar mean runs across the plot. An upward arrow from the dashed line to the professional mean is labelled 5.1853 higher and a short downward arrow to the white-collar mean is labelled 0.3218 lower. Professional incomes spread from about 4.6 to 25.9 thousand dollars; the other two types stay below 9.' width=614.4} ::: ::: The coefficients are 5.3741, 5.1853, and $-0.3218$. The intercept is the blue-collar mean, the dashed line in the figure, and each coefficient is an arrow from that line to another type's mean: professional occupations average 5.1853 thousand dollars more, white-collar occupations 0.3218 less. The fitted means, 5.3741, 10.5595, and 5.0523, are exactly the observed means, for the reason Chapter 8, Appendix A, gave: with one free parameter per group, least squares returns each group's own mean. A group-only regression is therefore a description of three means, with no adjustment in it. The figure also shows the wide spread of professional incomes, from about 4.6 to 25.9 thousand dollars, which Section 5 takes up. Keep this description apart from the full model. In `m2` the professional and white-collar coefficients are 0.3242 and 0.2353: they compare fitted incomes at the *same* education, prestige, and percentage of women. The raw professional advantage of 5.1853 and the adjusted 0.3242 answer different questions, and neither is "the effect of occupational type". ### Changing the reference level **Releveling** makes a different level the reference. Refit the group-only model with white-collar as the reference: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} group_fit_wc <- lm(income_k ~ relevel(type, ref = "wc"), data = d) coef(group_fit_wc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) relevel(type, ref = "wc")bc 5.052304 0.321832 relevel(type, ref = "wc")prof 5.507147 ``` ::: ::: The coefficients are now 5.0523, 0.3218, and 5.5071: the intercept is the white-collar mean, and the two coefficients measure the blue-collar and professional means from it. The fitted values and residuals are unchanged (Chapter 8, Appendix A); the same three means are reported in new coordinates. Releveling `m2` in the same way gives intercept 0.6559, blue-collar $-0.2353$, and professional 0.0889, while the education, prestige, and women coefficients stay exactly as they were. Centering a continuous predictor, subtracting a constant such as its mean, is the same kind of change: it moves the profile the intercept describes and leaves every fitted value, residual, and substantive contrast alone. Neither operation adds information, such as the cross-type support the records lack, and "the professional coefficient" always means professional minus whichever level is currently the reference. ### One-way analysis of variance as a regression Chapter 4 tested whether several group means are equal with a one-way analysis of variance. In the group-only regression, equal means says that both indicator coefficients are zero, so the reduced model is the intercept-only model, whose residual sum of squares is the total sum of squares about the grand mean. The test compares the two models' residual sums of squares: $$ F=\frac{(RSS_{\mathrm{reduced}}-RSS_{\mathrm{full}})/2} {RSS_{\mathrm{full}}/(98-3)} =\frac{(1734.0792-1138.123)/2}{1138.123/95}=24.8725. $$ The numerator is the drop in residual sum of squares that the two indicators buy, per indicator; the denominator is the group-only model's residual mean square on its 95 degrees of freedom. ```{=latex} \Needspace{13\baselineskip} ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(lm(income_k ~ 1, data = d), group_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Res.Df| RSS| Df| Sum of Sq| F| Pr(>F)| |------:|--------:|--:|---------:|--------:|------:| | 97| 1734.079| NA| NA| NA| NA| | 95| 1138.123| 2| 595.9562| 24.87246| 0|
::: ::: `aov()` returns the same statistic from the same fitted means, residual sum of squares, and degrees of freedom. The equality is algebraic: it holds whether or not group membership was randomized, so it supplies no causal warrant of its own. As in Chapter 4, the omnibus $F$ says that the three means are not all equal but not which differ, and a comparison chosen after seeing it needs Chapter 4's family calibration. The next section gives the calculation for a single declared comparison. ## Contrasts and Adjusted Group Comparisons {#sec-ch9-contrasts} ### A contrast and its standard error A **contrast** is a linear combination of coefficients, $C=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta$, declared before the comparison is read. Its estimate is the same combination of the fitted coefficients, and its variance uses the whole coefficient covariance matrix $\widehat{\mathbf V}$: $$ \widehat C=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat C)=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c,\qquad SE(\widehat C)=\sqrt{\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c}. $$ For a difference of two coefficients the variance reduces to $\operatorname{Var}(b_1)+\operatorname{Var}(b_2)-2\operatorname{Cov}(b_1,b_2)$. Take professional minus white-collar in `m2`, whose coefficients are ordered intercept, education, prestige, women, professional, white-collar, so that $\mathbf c=(0,0,0,0,1,-1)^{\mathsf T}$. ```{=latex} \Needspace{9\baselineskip} ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c_vec <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, -1) V <- vcov(m2) c(estimate = sum(c_vec * coef(m2)), SE = sqrt(drop(c_vec %*% V %*% c_vec))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate SE 0.08886278 1.07999307 ``` ::: ::: The estimate is $0.3242-0.2353=0.0889$ thousand dollars. Its variance combines the two coefficient variances and their covariance, $$ 2.1406+0.9698-2(0.972)=1.1664, $$ so the SE is 1.08 and, with $t_{.975,92}=1.9861$, the 95% interval is $[-2.0561,\ 2.2338]$. The covariance matters because the two type coefficients, both measured from the blue-collar reference, move together: their correlation is .6746, so a sample that overstates one tends to overstate the other, and their difference varies less than it would if the two moved independently. Dropping the covariance would give an SE of 1.7636, and adding the two standard errors, $1.4631+0.9848=2.4479$, gives a number that is not the standard error of anything. The vector $\mathbf c$ is the question written down. One entry set to 1 and the rest to 0 returns an ordinary coefficient. Entries on the type coefficients that sum to zero, with the intercept entry 0, make a contrast in Chapter 4's sense, which names the same comparison whichever level is the reference: the releveled fit of Section 1.3 also gave 0.0889. A contrast chosen because it looked large in the output needs Chapter 4's calibration for the family it was chosen from. Here the interval covers zero, so the records leave the comparison unresolved, and it remains a working-model calculation for types that barely overlap on the other predictors (Chapter 8). ### Testing a block of coefficients A contrast tests one declared combination. A **block test** asks whether a set of coefficients is jointly zero; it is Section 1.4's comparison of two models with a different reduced model. Two blocks ask different questions here. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} no_type <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women, data = d) anova(m1, m2) anova(no_type, m2) ``` ::: Adding the percentage of women and the two type indicators to `m1` tests three restrictions against the full model's 92 residual degrees of freedom; dropping type from the full model tests two restrictions against the same denominator. | Added | df | $F$ | $p$ | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Women and type | 3 | 11.5088 | $<.0001$ | | Type after women | 2 | 0.0319 | .9686 | : Two declared adjusted block comparisons. {#tbl-ch09-blocks tbl-colwidths="[40,15,20,25]"} The first block is strongly supported: $F(3,92)=11.5088$ against a 5% critical value of 2.7036. The second is not: $F(2,92)=0.0319$, $p=.9686$, against 3.0954. Joint evidence for the first block does not show that each added column contributes; the percentage of women could carry the whole block. The second result does not show that occupational type is irrelevant: once education, prestige, and the percentage of women are in the equation, the two type indicators reduce the residual sum of squares by almost nothing *on these 98 records*, where the types barely overlap on the other predictors. A single `anova(m2)` answers a different question. It gives **sequential** sums of squares: each line tests a term given only the terms above it in the formula, so the answers depend on the order of the formula, and only the last line matches a block test. Section 5.2 gives the robust version of the type block. ### Analysis of covariance {#ch09-ancova} The occupation types differ in many ways at once. A randomized study with a baseline score lets the group question be asked more sharply. Baumann and colleagues randomly assigned 68 fourth-grade pupils in one school to three reading-instruction conditions [@baumann1992]: DRA, a directed reading activity from the basal programme; DRTA, a directed reading-thinking activity; and think-aloud strategy instruction. Each pupil took an error-detection test of comprehension monitoring before and after the lessons. `carData::Baumann` holds the 66 pupils with a recorded first posttest, 22 per group. We use the first pretest and posttest, with DRA as the reference; the investigators also analysed further outcomes and both pretests. The **analysis of covariance** adds the pretest to the group comparison as one more predictor with a single slope: $$ Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\beta(X_{ij}-\bar X)+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \bar Y_j^{\,\mathrm{adj}}=\bar Y_j-\widehat\beta(\bar X_j-\bar X). $$ Here $Y_{ij}$ and $X_{ij}$ are the posttest and pretest of pupil $i$ in group $j$. The group terms $\mu_j$ shift the line up or down, and the pretest enters once, so every group's line has the same slope $\beta$. An **adjusted mean** is a group's fitted mean at a stated pretest value. At the grand pretest mean $\bar X$ it is the observed posttest mean $\bar Y_j$ moved along the common slope by the group's pretest departure from $\bar X$, the second equation. ```{=latex} \Needspace{20\baselineskip} ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reading <- carData::Baumann reading$group <- factor(reading$group, levels = c("Basal", "DRTA", "Strat"), labels = c("DRA", "DRTA", "Think-aloud")) ancova <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group + pretest.1, data = reading) coef(ancova) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) groupDRTA groupThink-aloud pretest.1 -0.5966478 3.6265538 2.0361644 0.6931872 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} predict(ancova, interval = "confidence", newdata = data.frame(group = levels(reading$group), pretest.1 = mean(reading$pretest.1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fit lwr upr 1 6.188185 5.143481 7.232889 2 9.814739 8.779995 10.849482 3 8.224349 7.181274 9.267425 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Posttest against pretest for the 66 Baumann pupils. The parallel lines are the common-slope fit over the common pretest support 6--14; each filled symbol marks a group's observed pretest and posttest means, and its arrow follows the group's line to the grand pretest mean 9.7879, where the open symbol marks the adjusted mean.](chapter_09_files/figure-html/fig-ch9-ancova-1.png){#fig-ch9-ancova fig-pos='!ht' fig-alt='Grey points for DRA (circles), DRTA (triangles) and Think-aloud (squares) pupils, pretest from 4 to 16 and posttest from 1 to 15, slightly jittered. Three parallel fitted lines with slope about 0.69 run from pretest 6 to 14: DRTA highest, Think-aloud in the middle and DRA lowest. A vertical line marks the grand pretest mean 9.79, where open symbols mark the adjusted means. The DRA mean, a filled circle at pretest 10.5 and posttest 6.68, moves down its line to 6.19; the Think-aloud mean, at 9.14 and 7.77, moves up to 8.22; the DRTA mean, at 9.73 and 9.77, barely moves, to 9.81, so its filled and open triangles almost coincide.' width=614.4} ::: ::: Read @fig-ch9-ancova from each filled symbol, a group's observed pretest and posttest means, to the open symbol on the vertical line, its adjusted mean. DRA happened to start highest, 0.7121 points above the grand pretest mean of 9.7879, so following its line to the grand mean lowers its posttest mean by $0.6932\times0.7121$, from 6.6818 to 6.1882. Think-aloud started 0.6515 points below and rises from 7.7727 to 8.2243, while DRTA, almost at the grand mean, barely moves, from 9.7727 to 9.8147. The fit gives the common slope 0.6932 (SE 0.1015), differences from DRA of 3.6266 (SE 0.7362) for DRTA and 2.0362 (SE 0.7450) for Think-aloud, and a residual mean square of 5.894 on 62 degrees of freedom. Tested together after the pretest, the two group coefficients give $F(2,62)=12.1689$, $p<.0001$; the adjusted means have 95% intervals $[5.1435,\ 7.2329]$, $[8.7800,\ 10.8495]$, and $[7.1813,\ 9.2674]$. Three conditions carry that reading. The adjusted means need a **common reference**, here the grand pretest mean. The reference must lie inside every group's observed pretest range, the **common support**: the pretests run from 4 to 16, 6 to 16, and 4 to 14, so the lines are drawn over 6 to 14, and a comparison read outside that band would rest on extrapolation. And the comparison needs a stated **averaging population**: for this additive model, predicting every group at the grand pretest mean gives the same values as predicting every group at each of the 66 pupils' pretests and averaging. Because the lines are parallel, the adjusted differences, 3.6266 and 2.0362, are the same at any pretest value inside the common support; the adjusted means are not, which is why the reference value is stated. ### Three analyses of a pretest--posttest study {#ch09-ancova-pretest} A randomized pretest--posttest study is often analysed in one of three ways: compare the posttest means, compare the gains (posttest minus pretest), or adjust for the pretest as above. The three are one regression that differs only in the pretest coefficient $\gamma$: $$ Y_i-\gamma X_i=\alpha+\delta_{\mathrm{DRTA}}D_{\mathrm{DRTA},i} +\delta_{\mathrm{TA}}D_{\mathrm{TA},i}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \gamma=0,\ 1,\ \text{or estimated}. $$ With $\gamma=0$ the model compares posttest means, with $\gamma=1$ it compares gains, and with $\gamma$ estimated it is the analysis of covariance. In R, `offset()` enters the pretest with its coefficient fixed at 1: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} post_only <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group, data = reading) gain <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group + offset(pretest.1), data = reading) ``` ::: Under random assignment the expected pretest difference between groups is zero, so all three analyses estimate the same average difference in posttest scores. Random assignment covered the 68 pupils assigned, while the analyses use the 66 with a recorded first posttest, so the argument also needs a complete-record condition, for example that the two posttests went missing for reasons unrelated to what those pupils would have scored, which the design does not guarantee and the records cannot check. \Needspace{14\baselineskip} | Analysis | Pretest coefficient | DRTA minus DRA (SE) | Think-aloud minus DRA (SE) | Residual SD (df) | |:--|:--|:--|:--|:--| | Posttest only | 0 | 3.0909 (0.9614) | 1.0909 (0.9614) | 3.1885 (63) | | Gain score | 1 | 3.8636 (0.7779) | 2.4545 (0.7779) | 2.5799 (63) | | Analysis of covariance | 0.6932, estimated | 3.6266 (0.7362) | 2.0362 (0.7450) | 2.4278 (62) | : Three analyses of the Baumann records as one regression. {#tbl-ch09-three-analyses tbl-colwidths="[24,18,20,20,18]"} The three analyses differ in precision and in how this sample's chance pretest imbalance enters. The pretest means are 10.5000, 9.7273, and 9.1364, so DRA had a head start of 0.7727 points over DRTA, about a quarter of the pretest SD of 3.0205 across all 66 pupils. The size of that gap is what matters. A significance test of it would add nothing: random assignment already makes any baseline gap a chance gap, so the test would examine a null hypothesis known to be true. The gap accounts exactly for the spread of the estimates in @tbl-ch09-three-analyses: each DRTA estimate is the posttest-only difference plus $\gamma$ times DRA's head start, $3.0909+\gamma(10.5-9.7273)$, which gives 3.0909, 3.8636, and 3.6266 (3.6265 from the rounded inputs). Estimating the coefficient leaves the smallest residual SD, 2.4278 against 3.1885 and 2.5799, and the smallest standard errors, because the pretest predicts the posttest with a slope near 0.7 rather than 0 or 1. The choice belongs in the analysis plan, made before the outcomes are seen, not after comparing the three estimates. \Needspace{16\baselineskip} ### Parallel slopes and the limits of adjustment {#ch09-ancova-limits} A common slope is a condition, not a finding. The check adds the group-by-pretest product block, which lets each group have its own slope, and compares the two named models on the same records: ```{=latex} \Needspace{11\baselineskip} ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} varying_slopes <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group * pretest.1, data = reading) anova(ancova, varying_slopes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Res.Df| RSS| Df| Sum of Sq| F| Pr(>F)| |------:|--------:|--:|---------:|--------:|---------:| | 62| 365.4307| NA| NA| NA| NA| | 60| 347.9697| 2| 17.46099| 1.505389| 0.2301931|
::: ::: The product block gives $F(2,60)=1.5054$, $p=.2302$, with group slopes of 0.4663 (DRA), 0.6868 (DRTA), and 0.8768 (Think-aloud). These 66 records do not distinguish the two models, which is not the same as showing that the slopes are equal. When slopes do differ, an adjusted difference depends on the pretest value at which it is read; Chapter 10 develops that varying-slope model as an interaction. What adjustment supplies depends on how the groups were formed. In groups formed by random assignment, the pretest only sharpens a comparison that the design already warrants. In observational groups, a fitted comparison at a common covariate value cannot balance what was not measured; a covariate measured with error under-adjusts, leaving part of the baseline difference in place (Chapter 14, Section 5.1); and a covariate recorded after the groups formed can remove part of the effect being estimated. **Lord's paradox** makes the point with intact groups that differ at baseline [@lord1967]. The gain-score analysis asks whether the groups changed by different amounts; the covariance analysis asks whether pupils with the same pretest ended differently. The two can reach opposite conclusions from the same records, partly through the regression toward the mean of Chapter 7, Section 7. Neither analysis says which question is the causal one; the design does, and Chapter 14 returns to what a design supplies that adjustment cannot. ## Comparing Nested Models {#sec-ch9-comparison} ### Comparing residual sums of squares Sections 1.4 and 2.2 used one idea. Two models are **nested** when the reduced model is the fuller model with some coefficients set to zero, and both are fitted to the same records and outcome. Extra coefficients never raise the residual sum of squares; the question is whether they lower it by more than noise alone would. The **extra-sum-of-squares** statistic compares the two residual sums of squares: $$ F=\frac{(RSS_{R}-RSS_{F})/q}{RSS_{F}/(n-p)}. $$ The numerator is the drop that the $q$ extra coefficients buy, per coefficient. The denominator is the fuller model's residual mean square, with $p$ its number of coefficients: the same $s^2$ that appears in every classical standard error. Under the Normal linear model with independent common-variance errors, the ratio has an $F$ reference with $q$ and $n-p$ degrees of freedom. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual sum of squares as columns are added to the occupation model on the same 98 records; each label gives the drop that the added column or block buys.](chapter_09_files/figure-html/fig-ch9-rss-1.png){#fig-ch9-rss fig-pos='!ht' fig-alt='Horizontal bars of residual sum of squares for five nested models. The larger value is not evidence that `m0` is better, because the two statistics test different restrictions. Neither checks the mean function, and neither says how a fitted rule would predict new records (Chapter 13). ### The same test in matrix form The statistic also has a compact matrix form. Let $\mathbf X$ hold $n$ rows and $p$ coefficient columns including the intercept, with full column rank. Least squares solves the normal equations $\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0$, so that $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y$, $\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf H\mathbf y$ with $\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}$, and $\widehat{\mathbf V}=s^2(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}$. For $q$ independent linear restrictions $\mathbf R\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf r$, $$ F=\frac{(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)^{\mathsf T}\, [\mathbf R(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}]^{-1}\, (\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)}{q\,s^{2}}\sim F_{q,\,n-p}. $$ For `m2`, $\mathbf X$ has six columns and rank 6: the two type indicators do not reproduce the intercept column, so every coefficient is separately estimable. Choosing the two rows of $\mathbf R$ that select the type coefficients, with $\mathbf r=\mathbf 0$, returns 0.0319, the type block test of Section 2.2, without fitting a second model. The equation explains what the estimator *is*, not how R computes it: `lm()` uses a QR decomposition, which is numerically better behaved than forming $(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}$ [@fox2016; @fox2019]. Because $\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf H\mathbf y$ is a projection onto the column space of $\mathbf X$, any full-rank recoding of a factor spans the same space and leaves the fitted values alone: Section 1.3's releveling result, stated geometrically. Appendix A carries the derivation. ### Information criteria: AIC and BIC A nested $F$ test compares two models when one contains the other. Information criteria can also rank models that are not nested, using a different quantity: the maximized likelihood, penalized for the number of fitted parameters. Chapter 8, Appendix B, built that likelihood for these models by carrying Chapter 6's binomial likelihood for 32 successes in 50 trials over to independent Normal outcomes around the regression. Maximizing it over the coefficients reproduces least squares. Its scale estimate divides the residual sum of squares by $n$, $\sqrt{RSS/n}=2.5373$, where the residual SD reported by `lm()` divides by the residual degrees of freedom, $\sqrt{RSS/(n-p)}=2.6187$. AIC adds $2k$ to $-2\log\widehat L$ and BIC adds $k\log n$, where $k$ counts the fitted coefficients **and** the residual variance, so `m2` has $k=7$, not 6. One call returns all three quantities: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(logLik = logLik(m2), AIC = AIC(m2), BIC = BIC(m2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` logLik AIC BIC -230.3020 474.6040 492.6988 ``` ::: ::: For `m2` it returns $-230.3020$, 474.6040, and 492.6988. Smaller is preferred, and both criteria prefer `m2`. The two criteria charge differently for parameters. For the seven parameters of `m2`, BIC charges $7\log 98=32.0948$ instead of AIC's 14, because at $n=98$ the factor $\log n=4.585$ exceeds 2, so the criteria can disagree; a disagreement shows how strongly the extra parameters are charged, not a tie to break by preference. The criteria are comparable only among models fitted to the same records, with the same outcome on the same scale, under one likelihood convention; Section 4.2 shows a change of scale breaking the comparison. Both are calculated on the records that fitted the models, so neither is a held-out error, and both are comparative: a smaller AIC says one candidate is preferred to another, not that either describes the records well [@akaike1974; @schwarz1978]. A single $s^2$ averages these spreads, so it overstates the uncertainty contributed by some rows and understates it for others. The remedy is already in hand. Chapter 7, Section 6.1, first used a robust standard error on the simple line (slope SE 0.1270 to 0.1491), and Chapter 8 applied the same HC3 estimator to the full model: its Section 3.3 made the `sandwich::vcovHC()` call, and its Appendix B gave the estimator, which keeps the design component outside and replaces the single $s^2$ inside by each row's own leverage-adjusted squared residual, with classical and HC3 standard errors for all six coefficients [@white1980; @mackinnon1985; @long2000; @zeileis2004]. The professional coefficient's SE grows by about 40%, from 1.4631 to 2.0928, as the wide professional spread predicts, while the white-collar SE grows by only about 7%, from 0.9848 to 1.0548. The education SE grows from 0.2752 to 0.3823, with robust 95% interval $[-0.6429,\ 0.8758]$: wider, with the same reading of an imprecise comparison. The SE for the percentage of women *falls*, from 0.0097 to 0.0079, so a robust covariance is not a penalty applied to every coefficient; it is a different estimate of the same target. Every coefficient, fitted value, and residual stays exactly what it was, because HC3 replaces a covariance estimate, not a fit. Switching estimators after seeing which gives the preferred conclusion turns a stated method into a selection. ### A robust block test The restriction statistic of Section 3.2 needs only a coefficient vector and a covariance matrix. Substituting $\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{HC3}}$ for $\widehat{\mathbf V}$ gives an approximate Wald version of the same block test: for the type block, 0.0345 with $p=.9661$, against the classical 0.0319 and .9686. Here the substitution changes nothing of substance, because the type coefficients sit close to the restriction, each within a quarter of its classical SE of zero, so both statistics are near zero and far below the .05 critical value, 3.0954. A change of covariance matters most when a statistic lies near its critical value. The two also differ in kind: the classical statistic has an exact $F_{2,92}$ reference under the Normal linear model, while the robust one has only an approximate reference, justified as the sample grows, not the exact finite-sample result of Section 2.2's test. ### Limits of robust standard errors HC3 has one job: under a linear conditional mean and independent observations, it estimates the coefficient covariance without assuming a common error variance. Several problems lie outside that job. - **Curvature.** If the mean function is wrong, the coefficients estimate a different quantity (Appendix A names it), and a robust covariance describes that quantity's variability without making it the quantity of interest. - **Dependence.** Rows that are not independent break the estimator's own derivation. Section 7 shows a robust row-level SE and a naive one agreeing closely while both understate the uncertainty by nearly half. - **Selection and causal identification.** Selection and missing outcomes change what the records represent, and causal identification comes from the design or from an argument about the conditioning set. - **Measurement error.** Error in measuring a predictor pulls its slope toward zero, by roughly the predictor's reliability when it is the only predictor, and no covariance estimator repairs it [@cohen2003]; independent mean-zero error in the outcome, by contrast, widens the residual spread and the standard errors but leaves the slope's target unchanged. Chapter 14, Section 5.1, develops attenuation. - **Thin support.** The type contrast's robust SE of 1.1827 is still the uncertainty of a comparison the records barely observe. A report therefore names the covariance estimator and the reason for it, and keeps these limits attached to the answer. ## Resampling the Records {#sec-ch9-bootstrap} ### Choosing what to resample Every uncertainty statement so far came from a formula: a coefficient covariance matrix, classical or robust, propagated through a linear combination. The **bootstrap** offers a different approximation: refit the model to many resamples of the records and read the spread of the refitted estimates directly [@efron1979; @efron1993; @davison1997]. What to resample is an assumption, not a default. - **Case resampling** draws whole records with replacement and refits. It inherits whatever unequal spread the rows contain, but it requires the resampling unit to match the sampling unit, with units independent and exchangeable. - **Residual resampling** holds the design fixed, resamples rescaled residuals, and adds them back to the fitted values. It assumes identically distributed errors, the assumption HC3 exists to relax. - **The wild bootstrap** also holds the design fixed but multiplies each rescaled residual by an independent mean-zero, unit-variance draw, so every record keeps its own error scale. This chapter uses case resampling, for two reasons. The occupation predictors were not designed: no one assigned education or prestige to an occupation, so treating the rows as jointly sampled is the natural view. And the residual spread differs by type (@fig-ch9-spread), so the identically distributed errors behind residual resampling are not available [@freedman1981]. Appendix B compares the other two schemes on the same targets. ### Case resampling for the full model Resample the 98 rows with replacement, refit `m2`, and keep the education slope. The seed and the number of resamples $B$ belong in the record, so both appear in the code; $B$ counts resamples here as it counted simulation repetitions in Chapter 5. ```{=latex} \Needspace{14\baselineskip} ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(90909) B <- 2000 boot_education <- replicate(B, { rows <- sample.int(nrow(d), replace = TRUE) coef(lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type, data = d[rows, ]))["education"] }) c(SE = sd(boot_education), quantile(boot_education, c(.025, .975))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SE 2.5% 97.5% 0.3698895 -0.6829568 0.7439809 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 2,000 case-resampled education slopes (seed 90909). And when a design has clusters, strata, or weights, the resampling unit has to follow the design rather than the rows, which is where the next section begins. ## Clustered Data: Project STAR {#sec-ch9-star} ```{=latex} \hypertarget{sec-ch9-star}{} ``` ::: {.cell} ::: The occupation records were observational, and the reading study was a small experiment in one school. Project STAR is a large experiment of a different shape: kindergarten pupils were randomized to class types within their schools. The randomization supports reading the class-type comparison as an assignment comparison, and the schools make pupils' outcomes dependent, which the uncertainty calculation has to follow. ### The study and its question The question is specific: > Among eligible kindergarten pupils in the participating Tennessee > schools, what was the mean reading-score difference under assignment to > a small rather than a regular class? The outcome is `readk`, an end-of-kindergarten reading scale score, and the field `stark` records the kindergarten class-type condition. Reading the small-versus-regular comparison as an assignment comparison rests on the documented protocol, not on the column name or the `lm()` call: random assignment occurred **within** participating schools [@finn1990; @mosteller1995]. The regular-with-aide arm lies outside this two-arm comparison and is excluded by design. Three limits come with the question. Class **type** is not a measured headcount, so the analysis estimates no dose response in pupils per room. The distributed field does not verify each pupil's original assignment; an assignment-effect reading also requires linking the recorded type to the assignment record and checking switches, which this teaching reanalysis does not do. And the target is the pupil-weighted mean assignment effect for the eligible cohort, which a common coefficient from a complete-record model reaches only through a further link: a common effect across schools or an explicit weighting argument. The data are distributed as `AER::STAR`, accompanying *Applied Econometrics with R* and following the version used by Stock and Watson [@kleiber2008; @stock2007]. They are loaded from the package, and the analysis is retrospective rather than preregistered. ### Which records enter the analysis A record can be absent from an analysis for two different reasons, and they are kept apart. Pupils who entered the study after kindergarten have no kindergarten condition: their absence is **structural ineligibility**. Eligible kindergarten pupils whose reading score or covariates were not recorded are **missing**, and missingness can distort a comparison. Only the variables a calculation uses enter its complete-record rule, so a missing mathematics score (`mathk`) does not exclude a usable reading record. \Needspace{12\baselineskip} | Stage | $n$ | |:--|--:| | Distributed records | 11,598 | | Kindergarten condition recorded | 6,325 | | Eligible small or regular | 4,094 | | Eligible, reading observed | 3,745 | | Complete primary records | 3,735 | | Primary regular | 2,001 | | Primary small | 1,734 | | Primary schools | 79 | : STAR eligibility and reading-analysis completeness. {#tbl-ch09-star-sample tbl-colwidths="[60,40]"} Of 11,598 distributed records, 5,273 have no kindergarten condition; they are later entrants, not failed measurements. The remaining 6,325 have a recorded kindergarten arm, and across all three arms 536 lack a reading score. Similar missing percentages in the two arms are reassuring but prove nothing, since the absent scores could differ systematically within either arm. Complete-record inference assumes that, given the declared covariates and within arm and school, whether a score was recorded does not depend on the score itself; the assumption is stated here, not verified. Among the observed-reading records across all arms, 38 lack at least one of lunch status, gender, ethnicity, and teacher experience; within the two focal arms, ten do. With $D_i=1$ for the small arm and 0 for regular, $$ \widehat Y_i=\widehat\alpha+\widehat\delta D_i,\qquad \widehat\alpha=\bar Y_{D=0},\qquad \widehat\delta=\bar Y_{D=1}-\bar Y_{D=0}=440.5474-434.7323=5.8151. $$ On the 3,745 observed-reading records the slope reproduces the arm difference of 5.8151 reading points exactly, as Chapter 7's binary predictor did for 24 pupils. The identity is algebraic; randomization adds the reason to read the difference as an assignment comparison. Two cautions attach to the number. Treating the rows as independent with a common variance, the slope's $t$ test equals the pooled two-sample test, here $t=5.6039$, which ignores that pupils sit in schools (Section 7.5). And raw arm means weight each school by its own arm-specific pupil count, so the pooled difference equals the pupil-weighted cohort target only under common assignment probabilities and comparable observation patterns, or after explicit standardization to target school weights. ### Adjusted and unadjusted models on the same rows The adjusted model adds free-lunch status, gender, ethnicity, teacher experience, and school indicators. The school indicators match the blocks within which assignment happened; the other covariates are the declared adjustment set, not a substitute for randomization. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} star_unadjusted <- lm(readk ~ stark, data = star_df) star_primary <- lm(readk ~ stark + lunchk + gender + ethnicity + experiencek + schoolidk, data = star_df) ``` ::: On the common 3,735 primary rows, the unadjusted difference is 5.8955 and the adjusted coefficient is 6.6575. Adjustment can improve precision when the added variables predict reading. It is not needed to remove baseline confounding that a well-implemented randomization already prevents; this is Section 2.5's point about randomized groups, on a larger design. Adjustment also does not automatically preserve the causal target: when the covariates were recorded, which rows enter, and what the fitted comparison compares still need scrutiny. The same-row pair is 5.8955 against 6.6575. Reading the report comes before judging it. In Chapter 1's argument components, applied as in Chapter 8, Section 7, the sample audit and the model code carry **STAT-E** content; the design and covariance reasoning supplies **STAT-J**; the estimate and its clustered interval supply **STAT-I**; and the first sentence is the bounded **STAT-C** answer. **SUB-E** situates the pupils, the test, the cohort, and the school context; **SUB-J** adds the assignment record with the selection and weighting qualifications; **SUB-I** reads the coefficient as an assignment comparison only under that support; and **SUB-C** bounds the substantive claim. These are linked functions within one argument. Judging the report separates what is *stated* from what is *demonstrated*. The randomization protocol is documented in the study's own publications; the selection and weighting conditions and the link from recorded class type to original assignment are stated here, not shown. The analysis of covariance adds a pretest: the posttest-only, gain-score, and adjusted analyses differ only in the pretest coefficient, and adjustment sharpens a randomized comparison without supplying what randomization supplies. Nested models on the same records and outcome are compared through their residual sums of squares, and information criteria rank models by penalized in-sample fit, never by held-out error. A squared predictor has no single slope, and a logged outcome asks a new question on a geometric-mean scale. HC3, the case bootstrap, and a clustered covariance each change the uncertainty for a stated reason and leave the coefficients alone; none repairs curvature, missing outcomes, weighting, or the absence of a design. In Project STAR, schools rather than pupils were the approximately independent units, and the standard error nearly doubled. Every comparison in this chapter was the same at every value of the other predictors, which is what "additive" means, and Section 2.5's common-slope check was the first test of that. Chapter 10 lets a comparison vary with another predictor and develops how to read, probe, and report such an interaction. \Needspace{14\baselineskip} ### Key terms {.unnumbered} Use this short reference to revisit the concepts introduced here. The exercises do not require it, and the Computer Lab carries the numerical reproductions. ### Projection and the normal equations {.unnumbered} Let $\mathbf X$ be $n\times p$ with full column rank, so $\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X$ is invertible. The least-squares criterion is $S(\boldsymbol\beta)=(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)$. Expanding gives $S=\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y-2\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y +\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$, and differentiating with respect to $\boldsymbol\beta$ yields the normal equations $$ \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0 . $$ The second form is the geometry: the residual vector is orthogonal to every column of $\mathbf X$. Hence $\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf H\mathbf y$ with $\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}$, and $\mathbf H$ is symmetric and idempotent, the orthogonal projection onto the column space of $\mathbf X$. Its trace is $p$, which is why the leverages $h_{ii}$ sum to the number of fitted coefficients; for `m2` they sum to 6. Two consequences used earlier follow immediately. Any full-rank recoding $\mathbf X\mathbf A$, with $\mathbf A$ invertible, spans the same column space, so $\mathbf H$ and $\widehat{\mathbf y}$ are unchanged: releveling a factor or centering a predictor cannot alter a single fitted value. Adding a genuinely new column enlarges the space and can change every fitted value. And under the classical error model, $\widehat{\mathbf V}=s^2(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}$ with $s^2=RSS/(n-p)$, which is where every classical standard error in this chapter came from. Solving the normal equations directly for `m2` reproduces `lm()`'s coefficients to about $10^{-13}$. ### General linear restrictions {.unnumbered} Let $\mathbf R$ be $q\times p$ of rank $q$ and consider $\mathbf R\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf r$. Since $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ has covariance $\sigma^2(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}$ under the classical model, the vector $\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r$ has covariance $\sigma^2\mathbf R(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}$. Standardizing by that covariance and dividing by $q$ gives the statistic of Section 3.2, which has an exact $F_{q,\,n-p}$ reference under Normal errors, because its numerator and denominator quadratic forms are independent chi-squares. It is the same number the extra-sum-of-squares formula produces. Minimizing $S(\boldsymbol\beta)$ subject to $\mathbf R\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf r$ with a Lagrange multiplier gives the restricted estimator $\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} -(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R^{\mathsf T} [\mathbf R(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}]^{-1} (\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)$, a correction applied only in the directions the restriction touches. Substituting it into the criterion shows that the increase in residual sum of squares is $$ RSS_R-RSS_F=(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)^{\mathsf T} [\mathbf R(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}]^{-1} (\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r), $$ which is exactly the numerator of the restriction statistic. Fitting the reduced model and differencing, or evaluating the quadratic form in the unrestricted fit, are two routes to one number; for the two type coefficients of `m2` both return 0.0319. Replacing $s^2(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}$ by a robust covariance in the middle of the expression gives the Wald statistic of Section 5.2. The algebra survives the substitution; the exact reference distribution does not. ### The HC3 sandwich {.unnumbered} Chapter 8, Appendix B, stated the HC3 estimator; this subsection shows where it comes from. Write the coefficient error as $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta =(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. Under independent rows with possibly different variances $\sigma_i^2$, its exact covariance is $$ (\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1} \Big(\sum_i\sigma_i^2\,\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\Big) (\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}, $$ a *sandwich* with the design component as bread and the error-scale component as filling. The classical estimator substitutes a common $s^2$, which collapses the filling to $s^2\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X$. The HC family substitutes each row's own squared residual instead. Because $E(e_i^2)=\sigma_i^2(1-h_{ii})$ under the classical model, the raw residual understates the error at high-leverage rows; HC3 corrects by dividing by $(1-h_{ii})^2$, which is deliberately slightly conservative and performs well in small samples [@mackinnon1985; @long2000]. Built directly from these pieces, the estimator reproduces `sandwich::vcovHC(m2, type = "HC3")` to about $10^{-12}$. ### The CR1 cluster sandwich {.unnumbered} Cluster robustness changes the filling, not the bread. Partition the rows into $G$ clusters and let $\mathbf X_g$ and $\mathbf e_g$ hold cluster $g$'s rows and residuals. The cluster score $\mathbf s_g=\mathbf X_g^{\mathsf T}\mathbf e_g$ sums the within-cluster contributions *before* the outer product is taken, so the estimator of Section 7.5 retains the within-cluster residual correlations that the independent-row filling discards. If every cluster held one row, the filling would reduce to the HC0 form, which is why a row-level robust SE is the special case that assumes away the dependence. The asymptotics are in $G$, not in $n$: 3,745 pupils in 79 schools supply 79 approximately independent pieces of information for this covariance, which is why the clustered SE of 1.8476 is so much larger than the row-level 1.0377 and why a $t_{G-1}$ reference is used. For the observed-reading model the finite-cluster factor is $c_G=1.0131$, and building the estimator from the school scores reproduces `sandwich::vcovCL(..., type = "HC1", cadjust = TRUE)` to about $10^{-13}$. ### What least squares estimates when the mean is not linear {.unnumbered #app-ch09-projection-target} A linear regression is often fitted where the conditional mean of the outcome is not exactly linear in the predictors, as Section 4.1's curved prestige component shows. Least squares then still estimates a defined target: the **best linear projection**, the coefficients that minimize expected squared error over the population the records represent, $$ \begin{gathered} (\beta_0^*,\beta_1^*)=\arg\min_{a,b}E\{(Y-a-bX)^2\},\qquad \beta_1^*=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}, \\ \boldsymbol\beta^*=\{E(\mathbf x\mathbf x^{\mathsf T})\}^{-1}E(\mathbf x Y). \end{gathered} $$ With one predictor the target slope is the population covariance over the predictor's variance, the population version of Chapter 7's covariance-to-slope identity; with several, it is the population version of the normal equations. The target is well defined, but it is an average: the projection slope of income on prestige in the additive model averages the curve's steeper and flatter stretches, weighted by where the occupations' prestige values fall. Its value therefore depends on the distribution of the predictors, and a sample with a different prestige mix would have a different target even with the same curve. It is a declared alternative target, not a rescue for a misspecified mean. HC3 standard errors remain appropriate for it under independent sampling, because the curvature the linear fit misses behaves like one more source of unequal spread [@fox2016]. ## Appendix B: Bootstrap Schemes and Intervals {.unnumbered #app-ch9-b} Section 6 used case resampling and said why. @tbl-ch09-schemes sets it beside the other two schemes on the same model, the same three targets, the same seed, and $B=2000$. | Scheme | What is resampled | Assumption carried | Education slope | prof $-$ wc | prof coefficient | |:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:| | Case | Whole records | Records independent and exchangeable | 0.3699 | 1.1187 | 1.9926 | | Residual | Rescaled residuals, moved across records; design fixed | One error distribution for every record | 0.2820 | 1.1081 | 1.4861 | | Wild | Each record's own rescaled residual, sign flipped at random; design fixed | Each record keeps its own error scale | 0.3673 | 1.1151 | 1.9767 | : Three bootstrap schemes for the full occupation model, with each scheme's bootstrap SE for three targets (seed 90909, $B=2000$). {#tbl-ch09-schemes tbl-colwidths="[11,27,24,13,12,13]"} Both design-fixed schemes rebuild outcomes from the fitted values.
